title: Sublethal pesticide exposure facilitates the potential northward range shifts of ticks by increasing cold tolerance and overwintering survival
content:
The extensive use of pesticides may drive complex interactions between species and their environments, leading to altered thermal tolerance traits and establishment in new habitats. Sublethal doses of pesticides may impact tick cold tolerance and lead to greater winter survival, particularly at northern range limits. To mitigate the risk of ticks persisting in previously unsuitable cold regions, we recommend adoption of integrative pest management approaches and reducing the use of pesticides. Importantly, our study assumed static pesticide usage over time, but reports suggest that pesticide usage is increasing. Limiting the use of pesticides and adopting integrative pest management approaches could mitigate pesticide-induced increases in tick survival associated with cold exposure.


Abstract

Pesticides are a primary tool for the control of harmful insects or other organisms throughout the world. Although most organisms are likely to encounter pesticides in the environment, little is known about the effects of these chemicals on the physiology of off-target species. We measured the impact of sublethal pesticide exposure on cold tolerance of two common tick species. We predicted that exposure to sublethal pesticides would make ticks more sensitive to extreme temperatures and investigated the population-level impacts by incorporating physiological survival data into spatially explicit species distribution models (SDMs). We found that exposure to sublethal pesticides increased survival at acute low temperatures, shifting the LT50 (lethal temperature at which 50% mortality is observed) of adult and nymphal D. variabilis from −16 to −19°C. During overwintering, significantly more ticks survived following sublethal pesticide exposure. Comparative analysis of previously published RNA-seq studies examining rapid cold hardening and pesticide exposure indicated potential transcriptional shifts associated with cross-tolerance between cold and pesticide exposure. Lastly, we demonstrate that pesticide-induced increases in cold tolerance may allow faster northward range shifts of D. variabilis. We also demonstrate that incorporating physiological data into SDMs moderates the estimated impacts of environmental change and may provide more accurate predictions of species responses to changing environments.
